description: Fig. 10 is a two-panel composite of tensile-property curves for Fe–30Mn–10Al–1.5C–xBe low-density steel rolled at 1050 °C, with the same four colour-coded alloys in both panels: 0Be (black), 0.5Be (red), 1.0Be (blue) and 1.5Be (green). (a) plots Engineering Stress (MPa, 0–1400) against Engineering Strain (%, 0–40) and contains an inset technical drawing of the flat tensile specimen with small dimensions labelled 50, 20, 10, 6, 3 and R5. The black 0Be curve reaches the highest engineering stress (peaking between the 1200 and 1300 MPa gridlines) and drops abruptly a little after 20 % strain; the green 1.5Be curve rises to just under 1200 MPa and drops at about 15 % strain; the red 0.5Be curve plateaus near 1100 MPa and extends furthest along the strain axis; the blue 1.0Be curve lies lowest (≈1080 MPa at ≈28 % strain) before dropping. (b) plots Strain Hardening Rate (dσ/dε) in GPa (0–5) against True Strain (%, 0–35): all four curves fall steeply from above the 5 GPa axis limit to a steady-state plateau between roughly 1.3 and 2.2 GPa, the 0.5Be (red) curve lying lowest and 1.5Be (green) highest before ending near 15 % true strain. Together the panels show that Be addition first lowers and then raises the steady-state strain-hardening rate while reshaping the strength–ductility balance.

observations.observation: Panel (a) axes are labelled 'Engineering Stress (MPa)' (0–1400, ticks every 200) and 'Engineering Strain (%)' (0–40, ticks every 10).
Panel (a) legend lists four alloys in the order 0Be (black), 0.5Be (red), 1.0Be (blue), 1.5Be (green).
In panel (a) the black 0Be curve attains the highest engineering stress, peaking between the 1200 and 1300 MPa gridlines, then falls abruptly a little after 20 % strain.
In panel (a) the blue 1.0Be curve is the lowest of the four, reaching about 1080 MPa (between the 1000 and 1200 MPa gridlines) at roughly 28 % strain before an abrupt drop.

In panel (a) the green 1.5Be curve rises to just below 1200 MPa and fractures at about 15 % engineering strain, whereas the red 0.5Be curve plateaus near 1100 MPa and extends furthest along the strain axis.
Panel (a) contains an inset drawing of the flat tensile specimen on which dimensions 50, 20, 10, 6, 3 and R5 are marked.
Panel (b) axes are labelled 'Strain Hardening Rate (dσ/dε) GPa' (0–5, ticks every 1) and 'True Strain (%)' (0–35, ticks every 5).
In panel (b) all four curves start above the 5 GPa limit and decay steeply to a steady-state plateau that lies between roughly 1.3 and 2.2 GPa.

In panel (b) the 0.5Be (red) curve has the lowest plateau (about 1.3–1.6 GPa) and the longest extent (to roughly 33 % true strain), while the 1.5Be (green) curve keeps the highest level but ends near 15 % true strain.

The caption describes (a) as 'engineering stress strain curves' and (b) as 'true stress and strain hardness rate' for steel rolled at 1050 °C; the wording for (b) is imprecise relative to the plotted axis label 'Strain Hardening Rate (dσ/dε) GPa'.

The citing text states that with increasing Be content the yield strength first increases, then decreases and finally increases, while tensile strength shows the opposite trend (initially decreases and finally increases).

The citing text gives the elongation of the 0.5Be alloy as 40.47 %, which the plotted red curve in (a) does not clearly confirm because the curve terminates inside the plotted strain range before the 40 % tick; the two readings are reported as stated and as seen, respectively.

The citing text states that after hot rolling at 1050 °C the yield strength of 0.5Be steel is higher than that of 0Be steel, attributed to solution strengthening by Be, and that this is consistent with 1.0Be and 1.5Be steels.

The citing text states that Be addition initially reduces the strain-hardening rate in the steady-state hardening stage and that the rate then gradually increases with higher Be content, which matches the low 0.5Be plateau and higher 1.5Be level seen in (b).
The citing text states that 0Be and 0.5Be steels are austenitic while 1.0Be and 1.5Be steels are dual-phase austenite (γ) + ferrite (δ).

subfigures.description: Engineering stress (MPa, 0–1400) versus engineering strain (%, 0–40) curves for 0Be (black), 0.5Be (red), 1.0Be (blue) and 1.5Be (green) rolled at 1050 °C. All curves rise steeply, plateau and then fracture abruptly; 0Be reaches the highest stress (between the 1200 and 1300 MPa gridlines) with failure a little after 20 % strain, 1.5Be fails at ~15 %, 1.0Be lies lowest and 0.5Be extends furthest in strain. Inset: drawing of the flat tensile specimen with dimensions 50, 20, 10, 6, 3 and R5.

Strain hardening rate dσ/dε (GPa, 0–5) versus true strain (%, 0–35) for the same four alloys, same colour code. All curves start above the top of the axis and decay steeply into a steady-state plateau between ~1.3 and ~2.2 GPa; the 0.5Be (red) curve is lowest and longest (to ~33 %), the 1.5Be (green) curve is highest but terminates near 15 %, the 0Be (black) and 1.0Be (blue) curves lie in between.

panel (a): the exact strain at which each curve fractures cannot be read more precisely than between adjacent 10 % gridlines
panel (b): the true strain at which each hardening-rate curve terminates is only approximate
